metadata.title: Teachers’ team innovativeness in TALIS 2018: An empirical and simulation study using glmmLasso for multilevel data

survey_design.weight_fields_interpretation: The study uses TALIS 2018 microdata for Korea, with teachers nested within schools (and principals at the school level). In the data preparation step, the authors explicitly removed weighting-related variables (e.g., SCHWGT) along with IDs and standardized scores, and then merged teacher and principal datasets to form a single analytic dataset. The modeling approach (glmmLasso, LASSO, elastic net) is a penalized regression framework that does not natively incorporate complex survey weights, and the manuscript does not report applying TALIS sampling weights in estimation. Therefore, results should be interpreted as conditional associations/predictive performance within the analyzed sample rather than fully population-representative estimates for all Korean teachers.

data.handling_not_reported_explanation: Plausible values are not applicable because the dependent variable is a TALIS scale score (T3TEAM) derived from confirmatory factor analysis of Likert items, not a PV-based cognitive achievement score. Missing data handling is reported: the authors used k-nearest neighbors imputation with Gower distance for mixed-format predictors, so the missing-data strategy is not a reporting gap.

sample_details.sample_filtering_criteria: Used TALIS 2018 Korea teacher and principal responses. The authors removed irrelevant variables including IDs, weighting variables, standardized scores, and administration/version fields (e.g., IDTEACH, PISASCHOOLID, IDLANG, IDCNTRY, SCHWGT, VERSION). Variables with 20% or higher missingness were excluded prior to imputation. Categorical predictors were dummy-coded; multi-category items were treated as grouped predictors (e.g., TC3G10 with five categories was recoded into four dummies and selected/removed as a group). After merging teacher and principal datasets, the final analytic dataset contained 571 explanatory variables and included 2895 middle school teachers and 163 principals.

confounders_identified.variable_name: Teachers can rely on each other
Lack of employer support for PD

main_findings.dataset_used: TALIS 2018 (Korea) teacher and principal survey, middle school (no grade PVs; T3TEAM scale score)
main_findings.performance_metrics: glmmLasso (Study I): RMSE mean 1.775 (SD 0.055) with 30.48 selected variables on average (SD 9.98); LASSO RMSE mean 1.771 (SD 0.081) with 92.41 selected (SD 133.82); elastic net RMSE mean 1.792 (SD 0.094) with 111.01 selected (SD 190.61). glmmLasso selected 14 key predictors at the ≥75% threshold with 13 positive and 1 negative association.
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using TALIS 2018 (Korea) the study leveraged joint activities across classes, work with teachers on standards, attend team conferences, motivate low-interest students, and collaborative culture mutual support to predict teachers’ team innovativeness (T3TEAM), finding that glmmLasso achieved comparable predictive error to LASSO/elastic net while selecting a much smaller, more stable set of predictors (RMSE ≈1.775 vs ≈1.771/1.792) and that most key predictors showed positive associations. This indicates that strengthening teacher collaboration routines and supportive school cultures may be a practical pathway for improving teachers’ team innovativeness, while shared responsibility for school issues may require careful implementation because it showed a negative association.

data.outcome_summary: The study analyzes TALIS 2018 Korea teacher and principal survey data (2895 teachers nested in 163 schools) to predict teachers’ team innovativeness using the TALIS scale score T3TEAM. Because the outcome is a Likert-based scale score (not PV-based achievement), the authors used penalized regression for variable selection under a multilevel structure, comparing glmmLasso against LASSO and elastic net. In the empirical study, glmmLasso produced predictive performance comparable to the competitors (RMSE mean ≈1.775) but selected far fewer variables on average (≈30.48 vs ≈92.41 for LASSO and ≈111.01 for elastic net) with greater stability. Across 1000 iterations, 14 predictors met the ≥75% selection threshold, with 13 positive and one negative association (shared responsibility for school issues). Missing data were imputed using k-nearest neighbors with Gower distance, and the manuscript does not report applying TALIS sampling weights, so findings should be interpreted as model-based associations rather than fully population-representative causal effects.
